questions.question: What is a primary key and what are its characteristics?
questions.title: Primary Key in Databases
questions.direct_answer: A **primary key** uniquely identifies each row in a table. Characteristics: NOT NULL, UNIQUE, one per table, automatically indexed. Can be a single column (surrogate key like auto-increment id) or multiple columns (composite key).

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking a table can have multiple primary keys — it cannot, but it can have a composite primary key
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Distinguish between natural key (meaningful data like SSN) and surrogate key (auto-increment id) and explain why surrogate keys are preferred

sections.title: Primary Key Examples
Key Points
sections.content:
- Primary key: unique + NOT NULL; auto-indexed; one per table
- Surrogate key: artificial auto-generated id (preferred — stable, simple)
- Natural key: real-world attribute like SSN or email (can change, avoid as PK)
- Composite key: multiple columns together form the primary key
- In InnoDB: primary key IS the clustered index — table sorted by PK
- JPA: @Id annotation marks primary key in entity class

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: A primary key uniquely identifies each row in a table. Its properties are: it must be unique across all rows, it cannot be null, and each table can have only one primary key. The database automatically creates an index on the primary key. A primary key can be a single column — typically an auto-increment integer or UUID called a surrogate key — or multiple columns forming a composite key. I prefer surrogate keys for most tables because natural keys like email or phone number can change, which would require updating all foreign key references.

followup_questions: What is the difference between a natural key and a surrogate key?
Can a primary key span multiple columns?
What is a composite primary key?

beats.text: A primary key uniquely identifies each row in a table. It must be NOT NULL, unique across all rows, and there can be only one per table. The database automatically creates an index on it for fast lookups.

Without a primary key, you can't reliably identify or update a specific row. If two users have the same name and email, which one do you update? A primary key guarantees you can always target exactly one row.

items: Surrogate key: system-generated, meaningless (id BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT) — preferred, never changes
Natural key: real-world attribute that's unique (email, national ID) — can change, risky as PK
Composite key: two or more columns combined as PK — used in junction tables (post_id + tag_id)

beats.text: In our blog's users table, id BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT is the surrogate primary key. Email is unique but is not the PK — emails can change. In the post_tags junction table, the composite PK (post_id, tag_id) prevents duplicates. In JPA, @Id marks the primary key field and @GeneratedValue handles auto-increment. candidates miss: in MySQL InnoDB, the primary key IS the clustered index — the table rows are physically sorted by PK. Choosing a random UUID as a PK fragments this index, causing slow inserts. Use BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT or UUID v7 (time-ordered).

items: Using a natural key like email as the PK — when it changes, every FK referencing it must update too
Using random UUID as PK in MySQL without understanding B-tree fragmentation

speakable_v2.cap: Surrogate BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT is the safest default PK — simple, stable, and fast for InnoDB's clustered index.

questions.question: What is a foreign key and how does it enforce referential integrity?
questions.title: Foreign Key and Referential Integrity
questions.direct_answer: A **foreign key** in a child table references the primary key of a parent table, ensuring referential integrity — a child row cannot have a foreign key value that does not exist in the parent. Prevents orphaned records.

interviewer_intent.testing: Foreign key enforcement and referential integrity concept
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking foreign keys are automatically enforced in MySQL — MyISAM does not enforce them
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain orphaned records and how ON DELETE CASCADE or RESTRICT options work

sections.title: Foreign Key Example
Key Points
sections.content:
- Foreign key: child column value must exist in parent table's PK column
- Referential integrity: prevents orphaned child rows (dept_id points to non-existent dept)
- NULL foreign key: allowed and means 'no relationship' (optional FK)
- ON DELETE RESTRICT: cannot delete parent if children exist
- ON DELETE CASCADE: delete parent, auto-delete children
- ON DELETE SET NULL: delete parent, set FK to NULL in children
- InnoDB enforces FK; MyISAM does not

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: A foreign key is a column in one table that references the primary key of another table. It enforces referential integrity — the database ensures that a foreign key value cannot point to a non-existent primary key. For example, an orders table with a customer_id foreign key prevents inserting an order for a customer that does not exist. You define what happens when the parent is deleted using cascade options: RESTRICT prevents parent deletion if children exist, CASCADE automatically deletes children when the parent is deleted, and SET NULL sets the foreign key to null in children. In MySQL, only InnoDB storage engine enforces foreign keys — MyISAM does not.

followup_questions: Can a foreign key be NULL?
What is an orphaned record?

beats.text: A foreign key is a column in a child table that references the primary key of a parent table. The database enforces referential integrity — it won't let you insert a child row with a FK value that has no matching parent row.
Without foreign keys, comments can reference post IDs that don't exist. Your application might not notice these orphaned rows for months, until a query returns null where a post title should be.

ON DELETE CASCADE: delete a post, automatically delete its comments too
ON DELETE SET NULL: delete a post, set comments.post_id to NULL (orphans the comment but keeps it)

beats.text: In our blog: comments.post_id is a FK referencing posts.id. If you try to delete a post with ON DELETE RESTRICT, MySQL rejects it until all its comments are deleted first. With ON DELETE CASCADE, deleting the post automatically removes all its comments — the cleanest option for dependent data. sharp edge: MySQL InnoDB enforces FK constraints automatically. MySQL MyISAM does NOT. If your table uses the wrong engine, FK constraints are silently ignored — you can insert orphaned rows without any error.

items: Using MyISAM engine in MySQL — FK constraints are parsed but not enforced
Using CASCADE without understanding that it can propagate deletes across multiple tables unexpectedly

speakable_v2.cap: Foreign keys are your database's first line of defense against orphaned data — turn them on and let the DB enforce your relationships.

questions.question: What is a composite key and when do you use it?
questions.title: Composite Key in Database Design
questions.direct_answer: A **composite key** is a primary key made up of two or more columns. Used when no single column uniquely identifies a row. Classic example: an `order_items` table where the combination of `order_id` and `product_id` uniquely identifies each item.

interviewer_intent.testing: Composite key concept and use case
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using a surrogate id for junction tables when a composite key is more natural
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain when to use composite key vs adding a surrogate id to a junction table

sections.title: Composite Key Example
sections.content:
-- Junction table for Many-to-Many: Student enrollments
CREATE TABLE enrollments (
  student_id INT,
  course_id INT,
  enrolled_date DATE,
  PRIMARY KEY (student_id, course_id),
  FOREIGN KEY (student_id) REFERENCES students(id),
  FOREIGN KEY (course_id) REFERENCES courses(id)
);

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Composite key: two or more columns combined form the unique identifier
- Use case: junction/bridge tables in M:N relationships
- Each individual column can have duplicates — combination must be unique
- In JPA: use @IdClass or @EmbeddedId for composite keys
- Alternative: add a surrogate auto-increment id and put UNIQUE on the column pair
- InnoDB: composite PK = composite clustered index

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: A composite key uses two or more columns together as the primary key. It is most commonly used in junction tables that represent many-to-many relationships. For example, in an enrollments table linking students and courses, neither student_id alone nor course_id alone is unique, but the combination of both is — a student can only enroll in a particular course once. The primary key becomes student_id plus course_id together. In JPA, composite keys require either the @IdClass or @EmbeddedId annotation. Some developers prefer adding a surrogate auto-increment id instead and using a unique constraint on the column combination, which simplifies JPA mapping.

How do you map a composite key in JPA?

beats.text: A composite key uses two or more columns together as the primary key. Each individual column can repeat, but the combination must be unique across all rows. It's most common in junction tables that resolve M:N relationships.

In a post_tags junction table, post_id alone can repeat (one post has many tags) and tag_id alone can repeat (one tag applies to many posts). But the combination (post_id, tag_id) must be unique — a post can't have the same tag twice.

items: Composite PK: PRIMARY KEY (post_id, tag_id) — combination is unique, each part can repeat
Both columns as FKs: post_id → posts.id, tag_id → tags.id
No additional surrogate ID needed for simple junction tables

beats.text: Our blog's post_tags table: (post_id INT, tag_id INT, tagged_at TIMESTAMP, PRIMARY KEY (post_id, tag_id)). The composite PK prevents adding the same tag to a post twice. That's valid, especially if the junction table has extra attributes and you want to reference it as a full entity from other tables. Pick composite PK for simple many-to-many; use surrogate ID when the junction table becomes an entity itself.

Using @ManyToMany in JPA when the junction table has extra columns — switch to @OneToMany + @ManyToOne instead

speakable_v2.cap: Composite keys are the natural fit for junction tables — they enforce uniqueness and act as both PK and implicit index.

questions.question: Should you use auto-increment integers or UUIDs as primary keys?
questions.title: Auto-Increment Integer vs UUID as Primary Key
questions.direct_answer: **Auto-increment int/bigint**: simple, sequential, small (8 bytes), fast for indexed inserts. **UUID**: globally unique across systems, 16 bytes (36 chars as string), random UUIDs fragment B-tree indexes badly. Use int for single-DB applications; UUID for distributed systems.

interviewer_intent.testing: Trade-off knowledge between int PK and UUID PK
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using random UUID as PK in MySQL without understanding B-tree fragmentation
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention UUID v7 as an ordered UUID that avoids fragmentation, and INT overflow (use BIGINT)

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Auto-increment integers are simple, small, sequential, and fast for inserts in MySQL's B-tree index because new records are always appended at the end. UUIDs are globally unique — useful when merging data from multiple databases or in microservices. However, random UUIDs cause B-tree index fragmentation because inserts go to random positions in the index rather than the end, which hurts performance. For most single-database applications, I recommend BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT — INT can overflow at about 2 billion rows. For distributed systems where uniqueness across databases is needed, UUID version 7, which is time-ordered, gives global uniqueness without the random fragmentation problem.

followup_questions: Why do random UUIDs cause B-tree fragmentation?
What is UUID version 7 and why is it better for databases?

questions.question: Should foreign key columns be indexed in a database?
questions.title: Indexing Foreign Key Columns
questions.direct_answer: **Yes** — foreign key columns should be indexed. They are commonly used in JOIN conditions and WHERE clauses. Without an index, joining the child table to the parent requires a full table scan on the child side. MySQL InnoDB automatically adds an index when you define a FOREIGN KEY constraint.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of FK indexing for JOIN performance
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that FK columns should be indexed or that MySQL auto-indexes FK columns
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that MySQL InnoDB auto-creates an index on FK columns but PostgreSQL does not — you must add it manually in PostgreSQL

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- FK columns used in JOINs: should always be indexed for performance
- MySQL InnoDB: automatically creates index on FK column when constraint is defined
- PostgreSQL: does NOT auto-index FK columns — must CREATE INDEX manually
- Without index: JOIN on FK column does full table scan on child table
- ON DELETE/UPDATE with FK: database must check child table — index makes this fast
- Also index frequently used WHERE filter columns in child table

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Foreign key columns should be indexed because they are typically used in JOIN conditions. When you join orders to customers on customer_id, the database needs to look up matching rows in the orders table by customer_id. Without an index, that is a full table scan. With an index, it is a fast lookup. MySQL InnoDB is helpful here — it automatically creates an index when you define a foreign key constraint. However, PostgreSQL does not do this automatically, so you need to manually create an index on FK columns in PostgreSQL. This is a common performance oversight when migrating from MySQL to PostgreSQL.

followup_questions: Does MySQL auto-index foreign key columns?
Does PostgreSQL auto-index foreign key columns?
What is the performance impact of joins on non-indexed FK columns?

beats.text: Foreign key columns should be indexed because they're used in JOIN conditions. Without an index, every JOIN on that column requires scanning the entire child table to find matching rows.
Most queries in a blog join comments to posts (WHERE post_id = ?) or posts to users (WHERE user_id = ?). If those FK columns aren't indexed, every JOIN is O(n) instead of O(log n).

Your InnoDB-built schema auto-indexed all FKs, but your PostgreSQL migration doesn't — suddenly all your JOIN queries degrade until you add the missing indexes manually.

Adding FK constraints much later on a large table — the auto-indexing still helps, but the ALTER TABLE itself is expensive

questions.question: What is a surrogate key and how does it differ from a natural key?
questions.title: Surrogate vs Natural Keys
questions.direct_answer: A surrogate key is a system-generated identifier with no business meaning (like an auto-increment ID), while a natural key is a real-world attribute that uniquely identifies a record (like a national ID number or email address).

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of primary key design choices and their practical trade-offs
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Always using auto-increment integers without considering whether a natural key is more appropriate, or vice versa
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss the stability problem with natural keys — if a business attribute changes, all foreign keys referencing it must be updated

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
When designing a primary key, you have two broad options: use a surrogate key or a natural key.

A natural key is an attribute that exists in the real world and naturally identifies a record. An email address for a user table, an ISBN for a books table, or a tax ID number for a companies table are all natural keys. They have meaning — if you see the value, you know what entity it refers to.

A surrogate key is an artificial identifier generated by the system with no business meaning. An auto-increment integer ID or a UUID are surrogate keys. They exist purely to identify rows in the database.

The main advantage of a natural key is that it's self-describing and you can often avoid a join. If you know a user's email you can query them directly without knowing their internal ID. However, natural keys have a significant weakness: they can change. If a user changes their email address and you've used email as a primary key, you need to update that value in every foreign key that references it. This is called the stability problem.

Surrogate keys never change — once assigned, an auto-increment ID or UUID stays the same forever regardless of what business attributes change. They're stable, but they add indirection: to find a user by email you still need to look up their ID first.

In practice, most modern applications use surrogate keys (typically auto-increment integers or UUIDs) as the primary key and enforce uniqueness on natural key columns with a UNIQUE constraint. This gives you both stability and data integrity.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Natural key: real-world attribute that identifies a record (email, tax ID) — meaningful but can change
Surrogate key: system-generated identifier with no business meaning (auto-increment, UUID) — stable but opaque
Natural keys have a stability problem: if the value changes, all referencing foreign keys must be updated
Best practice: use a surrogate key as primary key and enforce uniqueness on natural keys via UNIQUE constraint

followup_questions: When would you prefer a natural key over a surrogate key?
What are the trade-offs between using UUID versus auto-increment integer as a surrogate key?

questions.question: What are ON DELETE CASCADE and ON DELETE SET NULL foreign key options and when do you use each?
questions.title: ON DELETE CASCADE vs SET NULL
questions.direct_answer: ON DELETE CASCADE automatically deletes child rows when the referenced parent row is deleted; ON DELETE SET NULL sets the foreign key column to NULL instead, preserving the child row without a parent reference.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of referential integrity options and their practical impact on data
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using ON DELETE CASCADE everywhere without thinking about whether child records have independent meaning
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention ON DELETE RESTRICT as the default, and discuss the danger of accidentally deleting large amounts of data with cascade

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
When you define a foreign key, you can specify what should happen to the child row when the referenced parent row is deleted. The two most commonly used options are ON DELETE CASCADE and ON DELETE SET NULL.

ON DELETE CASCADE means that when you delete a parent row, all child rows that reference it are automatically deleted too. This is appropriate when the child's existence depends entirely on the parent. For example, order line items depend on their order — if you delete an order, it makes sense to delete all its line items automatically. A user's session tokens, shopping cart items, and notification records are all good candidates for CASCADE because they have no meaning without the parent user.

ON DELETE SET NULL means when the parent is deleted, the foreign key column in child rows is set to NULL instead of deleting the child row. This is appropriate when the child record has independent meaning but the relationship becomes optional. For example, if you delete an employee who is listed as the author of some internal documents, you might want to keep those documents but clear the author reference to NULL.

The default behaviour if you specify neither is ON DELETE RESTRICT, which prevents deletion of a parent row if any child rows reference it. This is the safest option because it forces you to explicitly clean up relationships before deleting.

A word of caution about CASCADE: it can propagate deletes silently across multiple tables if you have cascading foreign keys in a chain, which can cause you to accidentally delete far more data than intended. Use it deliberately and always test the behaviour.

sections.title: Key Points
content: ON DELETE CASCADE: child rows deleted automatically when parent is deleted — use when child has no meaning without parent
ON DELETE SET NULL: child foreign key set to NULL — use when child has independent meaning but relationship becomes optional
ON DELETE RESTRICT (default): prevents parent deletion if children exist — safest option
Cascading chains can propagate deletes across multiple tables unexpectedly — use with caution

questions.question: What is referential integrity and how does the database enforce it?
questions.title: Referential Integrity Enforcement
questions.direct_answer: Referential integrity is the guarantee that a foreign key value always points to an existing primary key value, enforced by the database engine at insert, update, and delete time via foreign key constraints.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of how foreign keys protect data consistency at the database level
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking referential integrity only matters at delete time, not at insert time
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that some frameworks (like Hibernate) can manage relationships in memory without database-level foreign keys, and the risks of that approach

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Referential integrity is the guarantee that every foreign key value in a table points to an actually existing row in the referenced table. In other words, there are no orphaned records — no order with a customer_id that doesn't match any customer.

The database enforces this through foreign key constraints. The enforcement happens at three points. First, when you insert a new child row, the database checks that the foreign key value exists in the parent table. If you try to insert an order with customer_id = 999 and no customer 999 exists, the insert is rejected. Second, when you update a foreign key column, the database checks the new value is valid. Third, when you delete a parent row, the database checks whether any child rows reference it — and depending on the ON DELETE setting, either prevents the deletion, cascades it, or sets the foreign key to NULL.

Without these constraints, your application could end up with orphaned records that break queries and cause null pointer exceptions in application code.

It's worth noting that some ORMs and NoSQL databases manage relationships at the application level without database-level constraints. Hibernate, for instance, can model one-to-many relationships without actual foreign keys in the schema. This gives flexibility but means you lose the automatic consistency guarantee. Any bug in the application layer could create orphaned records without the database catching it.

For most applications, enforcing referential integrity at the database level is the safer choice — it guarantees consistency regardless of what the application does.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Referential integrity: every foreign key value must point to an existing primary key in the parent table
Enforced at insert (new child must have valid parent), update (new FK value must be valid), and delete (parent deletion is checked against children)
Without FK constraints, orphaned records can accumulate silently
ORMs like Hibernate can model relationships without actual DB-level FK constraints — convenient but risky

speakable_v2.hook: Referential integrity is the database catching your application's mistakes before they reach production data.

beats.text: Referential integrity is the guarantee that every foreign key value in a table points to an existing row in the referenced table. The database enforces this at insert, update, and delete time, preventing orphaned records from ever existing.

Without referential integrity, a bug in your service layer could insert a comment referencing a deleted post. The comment sits in the database pointing to nothing, causing null pointer exceptions or missing data in your UI weeks later.

items: Insert check: new comment's post_id must exist in posts — rejected if post doesn't exist
Update check: changing a comment's post_id to a non-existent post — rejected
Delete check: deleting a post with existing comments — depends on ON DELETE setting (RESTRICT blocks, CASCADE removes)

beats.text: Our blog enforces referential integrity on comments.post_id → posts.id. Try INSERT INTO comments (post_id, body) VALUES (99999, 'Hello') where post 99999 doesn't exist — MySQL rejects it with a FK constraint error. This catches a bug in the service layer before bad data reaches the table. non-obvious: Hibernate can model @OneToMany relationships without actual database-level FK constraints. This works at the application layer, but any direct database access (admin tools, SQL scripts, other services) bypasses Hibernate and can create orphaned rows. Always add real FK constraints in the schema, even when using an ORM.

items: Relying solely on ORM-level relationship enforcement without actual FK constraints in the database
Disabling FK checks during bulk data loads and forgetting to re-enable them — orphaned rows sneak in

speakable_v2.cap: Referential integrity at the database level is always on, regardless of which application or tool touches your data.
